short: Mexico has no general AI law, but a decree published 14 May 2026 amends the labour and copyright laws so that AI use of a performer's voice, image or interpretation needs prior written consent and payment. General-law initiatives wait on an Article 73 constitutional amendment; the LFPDPPP of 2025 gives a right to object to automated decisions.
title: Mexico AI Laws
subtitle: No federal AI law: initiatives in committee, and the 2025 data protection law
body_html:
Status at a glance

No general AI act; one sectoral AI law in force. Mexico has no general AI law. A decree published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación on 14 May 2026, in force from 15 May 2026, amended the Federal Labour Law and the Federal Copyright Law so that reproducing, cloning or simulating a performer's voice, image or interpretation with AI needs the performer's prior written consent and payment; it is the first AI-specific federal rule to take effect. In the Chamber of Deputies, initiatives to issue a General Law on Artificial Intelligence (expediente 7550) and a General Law for the Regulation and Ethical Use of AI (expediente 8135) are before the Science, Technology and Innovation committee, whose deadline to report on them was extended to 31 August 2027. The new Federal Law on the Protection of Personal Data Held by Private Parties (LFPDPPP), published in the Diario Oficial on 20 March 2025, gives people a right to object to automated processing that evaluates them without human intervention. Verified on 25 October 2026 against the Chamber of Deputies' Gaceta Parlamentaria and its consolidated laws.

Who regulates and enforces

  • Secretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno: imposes the LFPDPPP's sanctions (art. 59).

Scope and reach

No AI statute. The LFPDPPP gives a right to object to automated processing that evaluates a person without human intervention and produces unwanted legal effects (art. 26, fr. II).

Core obligations

  • Obtain a performer's prior written consent, and pay, before using AI or any other technology to reproduce, clone or simulate their voice, image or interpretation; employment contracts must state the conditions and remuneration for such use (LFT art. 305 Bis). Parody, satire and creative imitation are excepted where there is no intent to deceive or to replace the artist's work (LFDA art. 87, as reported).
  • Respect the right to object to automated decisions (LFPDPPP art. 26) and the law's other duties on personal data.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Infringements listed in art. 58, fr. VIII to XVIIIA fine of 200 to 320,000 times the Unit of Measure and Update (UMA)LFPDPPP art. 59, fr. IIISecretaría Anticorrupción y Buen Gobierno
Repeated infringementsAn additional 100 to 320,000 UMALFPDPPP art. 59, fr. IVSame
Infringements involving sensitive dataUp to twice the amounts aboveLFPDPPP art. 59Same

What is coming next

  • By mid-July 2026: the LFDA regulations were due to be adapted to the May decree; whether that happened was not checked.
  • Any Article 73 constitutional amendment, which must precede a general AI law; the Gaceta is watched weekly.
  • 31 August 2027: the extended deadline for the committee's opinion on initiatives 7550 and 8135.

The 2026 performers' law, and the road to a general law

President Sheinbaum sent the labour and copyright initiative to Congress on 23 February 2026, presented by the Culture Secretary alongside a new Federal Film and Audiovisual Law. The Chamber of Deputies approved it on 7 April 2026 by 335 votes to 129 abstentions, then accepted seven changes from the Morena coordinator Ricardo Monreal, among them dropping a duplicate fine from the copyright law and rewriting LFT articles 304, 305 and 994 on employer fines; the Senate approved it by 66 votes with 23 abstentions and the decree was published on 14 May 2026. It reforms seven LFT articles and twenty LFDA articles, adds the term "dubbing actor" to the copyright law, states that the voice forms part of the right to one's image, gives Indautor wider dispute powers, and provides that in doubt the clause most favourable to the artist prevails. Mexican counsel describe it as sectoral: it does not regulate AI systems, only their use against performers. The Film and Audiovisual Law, which also touches AI dubbing, passed the Senate in April 2026 and had not been published when checked.

The general law is stuck on a constitutional question. Article 73 of the Constitution lists the Congress's powers and does not mention AI, so under Article 124 the subject is reserved to the states, and several states have already legislated. Monreal acknowledged in the April debate that Congress should have amended Article 73 before passing any AI law. Initiatives to do so have been filed repeatedly: Monreal's own, published in the Gaceta on 19 February 2025, which would add AI to fraction XVII alongside telecommunications; a 3 February 2026 initiative adding a new fraction XXXII; and a Partido del Trabajo initiative in August 2026. The Senate's AI commission under Rolando Zapata worked on a base text for a General Law to Regulate and Promote Artificial Intelligence during the ordinary period that ended in April 2026, with a national AI authority among its proposals, but nothing reached a floor vote, and in September 2026 the president's bloc said it would act once the constitutional reform passes. Commentators count more than 80 AI initiatives since 2023. The order of events will therefore be: constitutional amendment, then a general law, then changes to at least seventeen other statutes, as Zapata has described the sequence.

Last verified

4 November 2026, against the sources above. The decree's DOF reference is as Galicia Abogados cites it; the vote counts, the Monreal amendments and the article 87 exception are from the Mexican press and law-firm notes, not from the decree text itself. The Senate base text and the 2026 Article 73 initiatives are reported from the press and legal commentary, not read in the Senate gazette.
